mutations.because: **Re-anchored a second time, not re-recorded — and found by a sweep rather than by a gate.** SG4 (#483) moved this block under `columnPanels.editor` and SG4's own review remediation then wrapped that record in a `useMemo`, so the indentation went 14 -> 8 -> 10 spaces and the recorded before-text hit 0 occurrences. It was still 1 on `origin/main` at 31518cc5, so this anchor died IN this lane and nothing said so: `verify-manifests.sh` replays only the manifests a change touches, and SG4 touched `sg4.json` alone, so Rule 2 would have refused this claim forever the next time anyone asked for it. Same element, same place, same claim. Re-anchored by SG1: the step card this mutation was written against is deleted, so the same defect is now written against the Template section in the one scrolling column -- the same file, the same two synchronised stacks, and a shorter test that no longer has to walk to a step first. The disposition defect the plan forbids, in the shape a lane would actually ship it: the section form renders a stack TOO, so the rail and the Template section each hold one and every offer has two places to drift. It is still written in BriefEditor rather than inside TemplateSection because everything is already in scope there -- a hand-rolled copy in the section would need an import the mutation cannot add, and a mutation that fails on a module-resolution error is not evidence about the assertion. Two synchronised stacks LOOK correct: every control works, every derivation is the same one, and no existing test counts them. It is caught only by a count of MOUNTS, and only one written over something structurally part of any stack (the add-offer group) rather than over this lane's own marker, which a hand-rolled copy would not carry. (RS2 re-anchored this text two columns left: the editor's main column lost a nesting level when the rail moved out of the row into the shell. The mutation, its claim and its command are untouched — only the indentation of the anchor.)

The second copy of the compatibility table, in the smallest form it takes: an offer computed from the layers on screen instead of read from `addableKinds`. It is not obviously wrong on sight -- it produces a plausible list of kinds, in template order, with no literal vocabulary anywhere for the D121 scanner to catch -- and it is exactly the class of defect D124 exists to prevent, because it offers kinds already at their cardinality cap and ignores the shared text budget, so Save refuses what the rail offered. Caught by the file that MOCKS the derivation: asserting `offered === addableKinds(state)` would pass whether or not the call was real, which is the vacuous shape this repository has been burned by, so the proof replaces the derivation's answer with one no state can produce and requires the rail to say it.

"Video and Animated text are part of every creative and cannot be removed" -- the rule the brief names, deleted. Every row gains a remove control, which is the gating defect DESIGN.md 1.5 names read backwards: the surface offers what the boundary refuses, so the press dispatches, the reducer silently declines it (`removeLayer` is a no-op for a required layer) and the operator is left pressing a control that does nothing. Nothing throws, nothing looks broken, and the rail's own rendering tests would all still pass -- a row with MORE controls satisfies every `getByRole` that looks for one. Caught by the assertions that require an ABSENCE, plus the "why" sentence, which is derived from the same answer and disappears with it.

D139, undone: the selection reaches the document. This is the plausible version of that mistake -- a row click that both picks the layer and acts on it -- and it dirties a freshly loaded brief on a gesture that was supposed to change nothing, which is precisely why the decision puts the selection in local component state. The highlight still appears, so the selection tests stay green, and no network assertion moves either. Caught by the pair that reads the SERIALISED brief before and after the pick and then asks the unsaved-work guard, whose silence is the dirty flag (D67). The sibling test in that file switches a layer off deliberately and requires the guard to speak, so the silence cannot be a guard that never asks.

#469's defect, re-introduced through the third child of the same subtree: a freshly allocated props object per render defeats a `memo`-wrapped child even when nothing in it changed. Every fetch-count proof stays green -- `usePreviewFrame` has a content key of its own and does not care how often its component re-renders -- and every rendering assertion stays green too, because the tree drawn is identical; only the COST changes, and every layer row now re-commits on every character typed anywhere in the form, which is exactly what C3 says an always-on rail must not do. It was review, not the lane's own cost proofs, that caught this on #469. Caught here only by a render COUNT on the stack, whose sibling assertion (a layer edit DOES re-render it) rules out a memo that is simply frozen.

The selection held as a SLOT rather than as the layer. It is the obvious thing to write -- the tape's beat selection next to it is an index, so the shape is already in this file -- and it is wrong here for the reason `CopyTimeline.vo.ts` states for the persisted key beat: the operator can reorder the list, so an index does not keep the selection on the layer it was on, it moves it to whichever layer now occupies that slot. Nothing looks broken: a row is still highlighted, exactly one row, and it is even a row adjacent to the one picked. A layer HAS an identity where a beat does not, which is why the fix is an id rather than the retirement the beat selection needs. The `after` keeps a setter shim so the two retirement effects still compile and still pass -- this mutation isolates the FOLLOWS-THE-LAYER property and nothing else. Caught by an editor-level reorder that requires the pick to be on the moved layer AND not on the layer that took its slot -- the first assertion alone would pass if every row were pressed, the second alone if the selection had simply been dropped.

Found in review on #474 (PR-Agent and Qodo, independently) and this is HALF of it: the pick was never cleared when its layer was removed, so the stored id dangled. It happens because D139 is working -- the selection is deliberately outside EditorState, so nothing in the reducer clears it -- which is why the reset belongs where the selection lives. No rendering assertion can see the dangling id on its own: the row is gone, so nothing is highlighted either way. The test ADDS the kind back, where `addLayer` derives the same id from the same kind, and the stale id resolves to a layer nobody picked -- which is invisible until exactly that sequence and is what CC4's sheet would read. The mutation is a same-value write rather than a deleted effect so that ONLY this reset moves: the brief-switch reset below stays in place, and its own test stays green, which is the point -- a fix that shipped one of the two would pass the other's test.

The other half of the same review finding: loading another brief inherited its predecessor's pick. The layer-removal reset above CANNOT cover it, and that is the trap -- the canonical templates share their layer ids, so `accent` picked in one brief still RESOLVES in the next, the highlight survives the load and now names a layer of a document nobody is editing. So the clear is unconditional on the identity of the brief on screen (`loadedId` for a saved brief, `tempId` for a draft -- the pair `previewIdentityKey` already keys frame identity on). Caught by a test that changes the ROUTE id, which is how a brief is actually loaded (D37), over two briefs that deliberately share their layer ids: with a fixture whose ids differed, the removal reset would have cleared it and the assertion would have been vacuous. Same same-value-write shape as above, so only this reset moves.

Review on #474: the label that NAMES the html element editor was styled text. It looks identical on screen -- same size, same weight, same colour -- and every other assertion in the file finds it by TEXT, so a `getByText` proof would stay green through this. The cost is paid only by a screen-reader user, and only on the case the label exists for: a template holding two html layers, where headings are the thing you navigate between and two identical paragraphs leave you scrolling. Caught by queries on ROLE and LEVEL (`h3`, under the step's own `h2` from SectionShell) -- and by the two-layer test asserting both headings in order, so the level cannot be satisfied by one heading in the right place.
